items.stem: Which workload is the best candidate to move from JavaScript to WebAssembly?

options.text: A CPU-intensive, compute-bound routine such as image or signal processing
options.rationale: Correct: compute-bound hot paths are where Wasm's predictable, near-native execution helps most.

options.text: A few DOM updates that run once on page load
options.rationale: Light, occasional DOM work gains little and Wasm cannot touch the DOM directly anyway.
Trivial I/O work does not benefit from Wasm.
Styling changes are not compute-bound and gain nothing from Wasm.

items.explanation: Correct: compute-bound hot paths are where Wasm's predictable, near-native execution helps most.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about WebAssembly are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Wasm runs in a sandbox and cannot directly access arbitrary system memory or the DOM
options.rationale: Correct: Wasm is sandboxed and reaches the DOM and system only through JavaScript or host APIs.

options.text: JavaScript and Wasm can share data through linear memory
options.rationale: Correct: linear memory is the shared buffer used to pass data across the boundary.

options.text: Wasm fully replaces JavaScript in the browser
options.rationale: Wasm complements JavaScript; JavaScript still orchestrates and reaches the DOM.

options.text: Wasm is always faster than JavaScript for every task
options.rationale: Wasm helps compute-bound work but is not universally faster, especially with boundary overhead.

items.explanation: Correct: Wasm is sandboxed and reaches the DOM and system only through JavaScript or host APIs.

items.stem: How is a string typically passed from JavaScript into a WebAssembly function?

options.text: By writing its bytes into the module's linear memory and passing a pointer and length
options.rationale: Correct: complex data crosses the boundary through linear memory using a pointer and length, often via binding tools.

options.text: By passing the JavaScript string object directly by reference for free
options.rationale: Rich objects do not cross the boundary by reference without serialization into memory.

options.text: Strings cannot be used with WebAssembly at all
options.rationale: Strings are routinely passed via linear memory.

options.text: By rendering the string to the DOM first
options.rationale: The DOM is unrelated to passing data into a Wasm function.

items.explanation: Correct: complex data crosses the boundary through linear memory using a pointer and length, often via binding tools.
